title: TESLA and ContourGlobal sign long-term power agreement covering 1 terawatt-hour/year for Sterling renewable project
summary: Houston and Milan, July 28th, 2026 This is one […]
body_text: Houston and Milan, July 28 th , 2026 This is one of the largest solar-plus-battery storage corporate PPA ever signed from a single plant in the U.S., and it will be served by the largest renewable plant in ContourGlobal’s portfolio. Project Sterling is a hybrid solar PV + BESS project in Arizona. With more than 1.4 GWh of storage capacity (360 MW/ 4 hours), and 450 MWac of solar PV, the plant will deliver 1,000 GWh/ year (1 TWh per year) of renewable energy to Tesla via a long-term PPA with bundled electricity and RECs. Substantial construction of the project initiated in 2025 through off-site physical work of significant nature; on-site groundbreaking is planned for 2026 and COD for 2028. ContourGlobal today announced the execution of a large-scale, Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Tesla for Project Sterling, a landmark hybrid solar and battery energy storage project located in Arizona’s WAPA region, with firm transmission rights into California’s CAISO market. The agreement with Tesla covers ~1 TWh per year, representing around 90% of the project’s as-generated annual output, and will provide long-term renewable energy. Project Sterling is a large-scale hybrid project combining 509 MWp/ 450 MWac of solar PV with 360 MW / 1.4 GWh of battery energy storage capacity, with an expected annual energy output of more than 1.1 TWh. Once operational, it will be ContourGlobal’s largest renewable asset to date. Acquired in the development stage in December 2024, the project has since been reshaped by ContourGlobal’s in-house Business Development, Engineering, Procurement, and Commercial teams specifically to meet the offtaker’s requirements. Substantial construction activity began in 2025 through off-site physical work of significant nature, including procurement of major equipment in June. On-site construction is scheduled to commence later in the year, and commercial operation (COD) is targeted for 2028. “ After starting operations of our first renewable plant in the U.S. in 2025, we are now moving ahead with the construction of our largest renewable project globally, located in one of the country’s most dynamic energy markets” , commented Antonio Cammisecra, Chief Executive Officer of ContourGlobal . “Securing our biggest PPA ever – and one of the largest of its kind in U.S. renewable history – with an iconic customer like Tesla, a true symbol of the global energy transition, is a testament of our ability to deliver tailor-made solutions to our customer’s energy needs. This milestone represents a remarkable achievement of our commercial team which spearheaded a company-wide effort to strike a major deal like this one.” Strategic Location and Advanced Project Design Located in Arizona and physically connected to the Western Area Power Administration (WAPA) grid, Project Sterling holds firm point-to-point transmission rights to access California’s CAISO and will be pseudo-tied, enabling it to serve Tesla’s needs.

title: How to prepare a Juicy Marbles steak?
summary: A simple guide to get the perfect medium-rare filet mignon with a killer crust. 🔥
body_text: While there are many ways to prepare plant meat, we'll focus on the most basic - the standard "salt & pepper" routine. Pepper is optional. So is salt, but who are we kidding here. Step 1 - Seasoning Sprinkle salt evenly from all sides. It's good to do this at least 15 minutes before cooking, but 30-60 minutes is recommended. If you leave it a little longer the steak will absorb the salt into its depths, ensuring an even flavor. Plus, it gives you time to prepare all the sides in peace. Step 2 - Choosing a pan Choose a pan that is as small as possible. Just enough to fit your amount of meat. That way you don't have to use too much oil and also it won't escape to the sides, leaving the steaks dry. Fat bottoms are also a plus, as they retain heat and keep it steady. Non-stick never hurt anyone either. Step 3 - Cooking Heat the pan on a strong medium and add oil/fat of choice. Enough to cover the bottom. Be careful not to overheat, that will not only make the oil rancid, it'll also burn the crust of the steaks too fast. Bad juju! Once the pan is heated, place the steaks inside and cook them evenly from all sides. (For extra gourmet satisfaction while cooking, you can baste the meat, make naughty faces and call the steaks bad names.) Once you reach a royal brown, you have attained the signature Juicy Marbles crust and have reached the end. Or is it just the beginning? Good crust example - nice brown, crispy edges, minor char 😈 It’s that easy! Bon appetit!

title: Don Garlits: Father of Swamp Rat, UFO Enthusiast, and Unequivocally the Greatest Drag Racer Ever

body_text: We’re standing near the entrance of the Don Garlits Museum of Drag Racing, located in Ocala, Florida. It’s a comprehensive, full-day history lesson, packed with dozens of famous drag racing cars, many of them driven by Garlits, known to fans as “Big Daddy”—we’ll explain how he got the very appropriate nickname in a moment. We’re winding up a lengthy interview with him, during which we were dazzled by his ability to recall names, places, dates, and details from a career that spans 75 years. He is much easier to talk to than he was a few months ago. Garlits, understandably, was stone deaf, so you would shout questions. Once that no longer worked, he began using his phone, attached to an iPad—you would state your question, and the phone would transcribe it. He’d read on the iPad, and he’d answer. The process took a while. But he got a cochlear implant above his still-barely functioning right ear for Christmas, and you no longer have to shout. “He told me it was the first time he’d ever heard my voice,” a young museum clerk said. As I typically do, I’m ending the interview with a trademark boilerplate question: “Don, is there anything I haven’t asked you?” We are, incidentally, surrounded by members of the museum staff, as well as customers who did not know that their $22 admission would include an audience with Big Daddy himself. They all eavesdrop with interest. Garlits considers my question for a moment, then takes a half-step toward me. He looks me in the eye and says, in a low, very composed growl: “You didn’t ask me about the aliens !” I step back, shocked and surprised, but probably not for the reason you think. Oh, I knew about the aliens, all right, and I definitely didn’t ask about them. But did Garlits recall a particular story I wrote years ago? Just how good was his memory? And that almost under-his-breath growl—why did it sound so familiar? It clicked. Clint Eastwood. You know: “Go ahead. Make my day.” Maybe it’s a generational thing: Eastwood is 96, Garlits turned 94 in January. Garlits’ longstanding interest in aliens—extraterrestrials, flying saucers, Area 51, classified government secrets, and especially UFOs, which Garlits has personally seen four times—wasn’t that big of a secret, but nobody had written much about it. Long ago, 20 years or so, I learned that in addition to the expected, brand-friendly website of www.dongarlits.com, there was a second one, www.garlitsdon.com. Click on that one, and this is what it said: “Aliens: What You Never Really Wanted to Know! By Don Garlits, UFO Investigator.” It was page after page of what he had learned in his years-long investigation—personal experiences, interviews, history—all very entertaining, and it dovetailed with his adjoining assertion that the Apollo moon landings never happened. I wrote a story for a magazine that mentioned the website, and two days after it came out, garlitsdon.com disappeared. It’s still gone. Did I cancel his website? And did he remember that? Was he angry? Don’t think so. We talk about aliens, but merely friendly chit-chat. Over and done. The rest of this story will be about Don Garlits, not UFO Investigator, but The Greatest Drag Racer Ever. ISC Archives/Getty Images Big Daddy was there at the start. And against all odds, he’s still here. Garlits was born in Tampa on January 14, 1932. His father was an engineer for Westinghouse, who quit his job and moved south for his health. Growing up, Don loved cars, but it wasn’t until his shop teacher brought a copy of a 1949 Hot Rod magazine to class that Don’s imagination expanded beyond the basic cars-as-transportation concept. He took a genuine and immediate interest in the magazine’s philosophy and developed a revised cars-as-hot-rods world view. Or at least a Tampa view. Back then, drag racing was two cars, stopped at a traffic light, squealing tires down Main Street when the light turned green. You hoped there were no cops around, and you secretly prayed nothing happened that might qualify as a Rebel Without a Cause movie moment. You know—the driver’s education filmstrips that showed a mother pushing a baby carriage into the intersection, then skid marks, and finally two caskets, one regular-size, one tiny. Cool guys sneered when they watched the movie, but that sort of thing sticks with you. In June 1950, Garlits and his hot-rod buddies finally got a chance to do some informal but legitimate drag racing at the nearby Zephyrhills airport, a U.S. Army Air Force facility during WWII that was passed on to the town of Zephyrhills. Once a month, they’d close down a runway to use for drag racing. Garlits, and his 1940 Ford convertible with a Mercury engine, was at the head of the line. By the end of the first day, the fire was lit. Garlits constantly went in search of one less tenth of a second. One more mile per hour. Garlits began building engines and cars that would go faster and faster. A junkyard Cadillac engine soon replaced the Mercury in his ’40 Ford. About that time, he and his wife, Pat—they had met at a popular lake in 1952, and were married February 20, 1953—were driving to a planned picnic near Lake Wales, just north of Sebring, when they spotted a sign that said “Drags Today,” with an arrow pointing down the dirt road leading to the drag strip. They detoured and never made it to the picnic. Garlits won his first trophy. Yes, he still has it. Garlits at rest—an unusual sight—in his office at the Don Garlits Museum of Drag Racing in Ocala, Florida, 50 miles south of Gainesville. Cameron Neveu If the drag-racing fire was lit in 1950, by 1954, it was raging. Garlits was never satisfied, always planning his next mechanical move. There was a ’36 Ford coupe, then a 1927 T roadster with a Mercury engine that he built under a tree in the front yard. He correctly reasoned that extra weight was a bad thing, so he stripped the T of everything but the body. Then one day, the body went. Meanwhile, drag racing was getting respectable. The National Hot Rod Association, the drag equivalent of NASCAR, was formed by Wally Parks, then the editor of Hot Rod magazine. This year, the NHRA is celebrating its 75th anniversary, beginning in March with the Gatornationals in Gainesville, Florida, right up the road from Garlits’ museum. By 1957, he and his friends had massaged their on-the-fly design into an approximation of a slingshot dragster—the driver was in the very back, legs straddling the transmission. The engine, a Chrysler Hemi, had been moved as far to the rear as it would go. Bigger tires were mounted inches from the driver. Frame rails from a junkyard ’31 Chevrolet cradled the engine and led to the skinny front tires. It did, indeed, look a little like a cocked slingshot. And like the dragsters in Hot Rod. Garlits wanted a car that was proper-looking, a representative for his business, Don’s Speed Shop, which was painted in big letters on the side of the dragster. The rest of the car was gloss black, a consistent Garlits trademark, as was a gold cross painted right in front of the cockpit. On November 10, 1957, the dragster went 176.4 mph and covered the quarter-mile in 8.79 seconds. Cameron Neveu Garlits had built and driven the world’s fastest dragster, and the first one to top 170 mph. That this occurred in Florida, and not California or at least in Detroit, caused much peeing of pants in the national drag-racing community. Garlits and his car were getting so much publicity that a racer from Detroit began posting disparaging comments in drag-racing publications, starting a semi-friendly feud, and claiming that Garlits was nothing but a “swamp rat” from Florida. Garlits liked the name, and his car was christened the Swamp Rat 1. With each new car, that number would increase by one. Ed Iskenderian , who owned a camshaft-grinding company south of Los Angeles and was a legendary entrepreneur and pot-stirrer, placed ads in magazines like Hot Rod and racing weeklies like Drag News touting Garlits’ ever-increasing performance benchmarks, invariably insisting that Isky Cams were one big reason for his success, especially at the expense of the California contingent. Iskenderian died in February at 104; when I talked to him last September, he told me to give Garlits his regards. Garlits’ fame spread from coast to coast, but he had yet to race farther west than Texas, and eventually he, wife Pat, and little brother Ed made the trip to California. It was humbling, a learning experience. But the next time they went back, Garlits dominated. Cameron Neveu Garlits’ fame continued to expand, though the cars slowed down—the NHRA instituted a gasoline-only rule from 1958 to 1964, but still Garlits went fast even without nitromethane. In 1962, he was racing at Indianapolis, a tough town. He’d gone there with Pat and their two young daughters, and the other racers began calling him “Daddy” Garlits. When Garlits won, the announcer, Bernie Partridge, said on the microphone, “Guess we’ll have to call him ‘Big Daddy’ now!” The Indianapolis newspaper picked it up, and the name stuck. For much of his career, Garlits followed the money, cherry-picking rather than chasing season championships. He raced with the NHRA, the IHRA, the AHRA, and anywhere else he felt like running: Big Daddy was always welcome. Well, by promoters; racers weren’t always so pleased to see him. All the while, Garlits couldn’t stop thinking, couldn’t quit innovating, constantly went in search of one less tenth of a second, one more mile per hour. Alvis Upitis/Getty Images Sometimes it got him in trouble. On March 8, 1970, at Lions Drag Strip outside Los Angeles, he was racing the Swamp Rat XIII, a conventional slingshot—driver in the back, engine just ahead of him, and straddling the transmission. This transmission was an experimental two-speed unit that Garlits was trying to perfect. As he was leaving the starting line under full power, on the final run of the day, the transmission exploded. The dragster broke apart right behind the engine. The rear portion of the Swamp Rat, where Garlits was sitting, levered straight up, into a 90-degree angle from the car, then slammed onto the pavement, separated from the engine and the rest of the car. The explosion sent hot oil and metal shards into the crowd, nearly severing a teenage boy’s arm. And the splintered transmission cut off half of Garlits’ right foot. It was bad. Compounding it, the ambulance crew slammed the door on what remained of his foot. He was out for the rest of the season. It wasn’t an entirely new idea, but it wasn’t until Garlits lost part of his right foot in this exploding-transmission incident at Lions Drag Strip near Los Angeles in 1970 that he was compelled to perfect a rear-engine car that moved the drivetrain behind the driver. It turned out to be better in every way. The Denver Post/Getty Images While he was in the hospital, he began designing a rear-engine dragster, where any catastrophic drivetrain failure would occur behind the driver, not in front. That design had been tried multiple times before but had always failed. Back in Florida, moving around his shop in a wheelchair, Garlits and his crew of T. C. Lemons and Connie Swingle started work on Swamp Rat XIV. To no one’s surprise, Garlits lost in the first round when he debuted the car back at Lions Drag Strip the next season. But Garlits is an unopposed genius when it comes to figuring out what’s wrong and fixing it, and soon he started winning, and by the end of 1971, the advantage of a rear-engine Top Fuel dragster was apparent to everyone. Within a couple of years, most every new Top Fuel dragster was rear-engined. By 1986, Garlits was up to Swamp Rat XXX, and it was performing remarkably well, winning the NHRA championship, the first dragster to top 270 mph. (Note that Garlits was also the first piston-powered drag racer to go 180, 200, 240, and 250 mph. Jet-powered dragsters had gone faster, but they were exhibition-only.) The nose of XXX had a snake’s head appearance, flaring out around the tiny front wheels, then angling down, designed to maximize aerodynamics. Racing in the NHRA Summernationals at Englishtown, New Jersey, the front wheels lifted slightly off the pavement as Garlits launched, but he kept his foot on the accelerator, eager to beat fellow Florida racer Darrell Gwynn, just starting his career. Suddenly, about halfway down the track, the front wheels lifted even more. Air caught under that wide nose and blew the car straight up, pointing at the sky, as even the rear wheels briefly left the ground. Swamp Rat XXX rotated 180 degrees and slammed down onto the asphalt, aiming back toward the starting line. Swamp Rat XXX does a “blowover” in Englishtown, New Jersey. It happened a second time in Spokane, Washington. ISC Archives/Getty Images The engine was still running, and the car drove out through a cloud of smoke, Hollywood-like, made a slight left turn, and stopped. Garlits, shaken, emerged from the car. The crowd exploded into cheers and applause, convinced Garlits drove out of that cloud on purpose, ever the showman. But he said later he was simply a passenger and had no control over what happened. “What those people witnessed was a 20th-century miracle,” he said. “My guardian angel looking after me.” Swamp Rat XXX went to the Smithsonian. A second, and even worse, blowover crash happened a year later at Spokane, Washington. Garlits had some injuries but healed up and then retired to the television booth to become a commentator. He attempted a comeback a few years later but had to quit after a race in Atlanta in April 1992, when detached retinas in both eyes made him see spots. It was caused not by the launch of his Top Fuel dragster, but by the deceleration, the 4g shock that occurs when twin parachutes unfurl at the finish line to jerk the dragster to a stop. Doctors told him he would be risking the loss of his sight completely if he continued racing. Still, he qualified for a few more races, the last in 2003, when he was 71. His best speed: just over 323 mph. More recently, he built an electric dragster, hoping to be the first to hit 200 mph. Swamp Rat 38 went 189 mph, and that’s all it would do. Not bad for an 87-year-old driver. Lately, Garlits has been staying closer to home, which isn’t far from the museum, though it’s likely he’ll do some personal appearances for the NHRA’s 75th. That museum is a revelation: Garlits either saved or bought back many of his historic cars, and he has displayed not only them, but cars made famous by other racers, including inventory from other forms of motorsports. That the museum even exists is literally an answered prayer, he says. Garlits’ first attempt at being a museum curator failed: He built it so far off the beaten path, on his family homestead, that nobody could find it. Wife Pat said that to succeed, it needed to be located off either Interstate 4, which runs from Tampa to Daytona Beach, or even better on I-75, which starts in South Florida and ends in Northern Michigan, at the border to Canada. Pat added up how much they could spend on land located near an I-75 exit: “She told me we could write a check for $80,000,” Garlits says. They knelt by their bedside and prayed. They began looking for land, but what they found started in six figures, often ended in seven. They made one more trip north on I-75 and pulled off at an exit south of Ocala. There was nothing there but a gas station and a turquoise-roofed Stuckey’s. But there was vacant land there that would be perfect. A tiny cardboard sign in a ditch said it was for sale and listed a phone number. They drove to Stuckey’s and made a phone call. A surly woman answered: Yes, it was for sale. “How much?” Garlits asked. “It’s $80,000,” she said. Not long after, Garlits was walking his property when a man approached him at the fence line. “I own this property next to yours,” the man said, “and I’d like to buy your land. I’ll give you $180,000.” Garlits told him it wasn’t for sale at any price. The man asked why: “Because God found this land for us,” Garlits replied. The man’s last name was du Pont. Yes, he was one of those du Ponts. The museum opened in March 1984. It’s located on 16 acres, and the display area has grown from 10,000 square feet to 65,000. Cameron Neveu Garlits has an office there, and a garage where he can work on his cars. Unless he’s on the road, he is in the office or the garage most every day. “See those file cabinets over there? They hold all my personal racing pictures,” he said, pointing behind his desk. “And they are filled up. Thirty-eight Swamp Rats, and there were cars before we started naming them. My 1940 Fords, my ’36 Fords, my roadsters, my flathead dragsters, and then we get to the Swamp Rats. I’m in the process of scanning all those files, and I’m down now to the third drawer over on the far side, up to 1984. I’m trying to identify every picture—it’s easy telling what the car is, but it’s a lot harder to figure out where the car is—sometimes I’m looking for some little clue in the photo that gives it away. I’m putting all those pictures on my little Samsung hard drive. “On top of that, I’m in the process of writing my life story— Don Garlits, The Official Autobiography —I’m at 85,800 words, and I’m up to 1987, and I’m just getting ready to have the big wreck that took me out of racing.” There have been multiple books written about Garlits. It will be interesting to see his own take. Staying busy is important to Garlits, and one of his answers to the inevitable question: What’s your secret? Cameron Neveu “I can’t stop working. You stop working, you die,” he said. There are so many memories, bittersweet ones. Garlits lost his wife, Pat, in 2014. They were married for 61 years. “She was the love of my life,” he said. A man isn’t supposed to outlive his wife: Ask me how I know. His younger brother, Ed, died in 2020. Most of his friends are gone. From his high school graduating class in Tampa, he is one of two who “are still vertical,” he said. Garlits has, at least, retained his sense of humor. “You have to keep moving, use every part of your body,” he observes. Including, as it turns out, the penis. “It’ll shrink right up!” he says. He knows this because “I’ve seen it with my own eyes!” No, not on Garlits, but on his brother, who was in a nursing home. “He had a nice one. But one day they were changing his diaper. All he had left was this little button! You’ve got to use everything, or you’ll lose it. “Sorry,” he says, “but the filter’s gone at 94. I just say whatever in the hell I want.” Cameron Neveu Garlits also advises fiscal responsibility. “I’ve got to save for my future! I’m going to be old someday! I’m not going to any nursing home, I’m gonna have a private nurse come to my house and take care of me, 24 hours, around the clock.” He laughs. We all do. I first interviewed Garlits 48 years ago at the long-gone Hallsville Drag Strip, located right outside the town of Hallsville in East Texas. Like a lot of the top drag racers back then, Garlits often did match races at smaller tracks around the country to earn extra money, maybe $2500 a weekend, when the major series were taking a weekend off. To draw a good crowd, the promoter for a second-tier track, where the usual participants raced hot-rodded, home-built ’55 Chevrolets or Ford Mustangs or Pontiac GTOs, would hire a pair of big-name drivers to match race each other in their 2000-hp Top Fuel cars. On this particular weekend, in April 1978, Garlits raced Paul Savadin, the owner of Paul’s Crank Shop in Devine, Texas, near San Antonio. Savadin may not have been nationally famous like Garlits, but he was well known in Texas and regarded as one of the best crankshaft guys around—he built them for Garlits. It was billed as the local boy takes on Big Daddy and—well, loses. But even then, it made for good bragging rights for Savadin, comparable to the time East Texas boxer Donnie Fleeman stepped into the ring with Muhammad Ali—who was still Cassius Clay then—in February 1961. Fleeman was knocked out and promptly retired, but lived another 50 years after that fight, plenty of time to let everybody in Midlothian, Texas, know that their Donnie Fleeman was the first pro fighter to last seven rounds with the soon-to-be Greatest Of All Time. In 1967, Garlits grew a beard, vowing not to shave until he ran the quarter-mile in less than 7 seconds. He finally did in September when he ran a 6.77 at the U.S. Nationals in Indianapolis, where he shaved on the starting line, surrounded by fans. ISC Archives/Getty Images Garlits today at 94. Cameron Neveu Don Garlits is to drag racing what Muhammad Ali is to boxing: the best. The difference is that pro boxing as we know it has been around since 1882, when John L. Sullivan became the first American heavyweight champion. A popular joke suggests that drag racing began when the second car was built, but the hobby became a sport in 1951, when Hot Rod magazine editor Wally Parks founded the National Hot Rod Association. The NHRA’s 75th celebration began at the Gatornationals on March 8 and will conclude 19 races later at the NHRA Finals in Pomona, California, on November 15. We’re 108 years too late to hear John L. Sullivan talk about the early days of boxing, but we still have Don Garlits to talk about the birth of professional drag racing. And, of course, UFOs. May the force be with you, Big Daddy. This story first appeared in the America 250 digital issue of Hagerty Drivers Club magazine. title: 5 Best RFP Software Platforms in July 2026
summary: In July 2026, these 5 RFP software platforms stand out for federal contractors managing compliance, pricing, and proposal workflows.
body_text: The rfp software market has a lot of options, but most of them were built with commercial teams in mind. For government contractors, that matters. You're tracking Section L requirements, building a compliance matrix, aligning past performance, and doing all of it under a deadline with a lean team. These five platforms cover a range of use cases, and we're breaking down each one so you can make a clear call on what fits your work. TL;DR Most commercial RFP software has no native understanding of Sections L/M, FAR/DFARS, or compliance matrix logic, which leaves federal contractors doing that mapping manually. Assess RFP software across five criteria: GovCon feature depth, AI citation quality, BD lifecycle coverage, federal security posture, and federal ecosystem integrations. Point solutions like Rohirrim and Procurement Sciences cover proposal writing well, but stop there. You will need separate systems for pipeline, pricing, and contract management. GovDash covers the full BD lifecycle from opportunity discovery through post-award, with compliance matrices that auto-update when amendments drop and Pricer extracting CLINs and LCATs directly from solicitation sections. What Is RFP Software? RFP software helps organizations manage and automate their responses to Requests for Proposals, Requests for Information, and similar procurement documents. At its core, the category covers tools that speed up the process of producing compliant, submission-ready responses, whether for a commercial vendor relationship or a federal solicitation with hundreds of requirements. For government contractors, the category splits pretty sharply. General-purpose RFP tools work well for commercial bids with relatively straightforward response requirements. Federal contracting is a different animal. A government solicitation can run 300 pages, span multiple sections with cross-referencing requirements, and demand a compliance matrix, past performance citations, labor category alignment, and pricing schedules, all before you write a single narrative section. That's why GovCon-focused RFP software tends to cover more ground: full BD lifecycle support from opportunity discovery through post-award, going well beyond AI proposal development . How We Ranked These RFP Software Options Rankings here are based on publicly available product information, documented capabilities, and fit for government contracting work. These assessments draw from product documentation, feature announcements, and known GovCon use cases without hands-on testing of every product listed. Five criteria shaped the evaluation: GovCon feature depth: whether the product parses Sections L, M, and C; generates a compliance matrix; and ingests solicitation documents without manual setup AI output quality: source-linked citations versus generic content suggestions that require manual fact-checking BD lifecycle coverage: how far the product extends across the pursuit lifecycle, from opportunity discovery through post-award contract management Federal security posture: FedRAMP status, CUI handling, and GovCloud deployment options Federal ecosystem integrations: connections to SAM.gov, GSA eBuy, GovWin IQ, and SharePoint Best Overall RFP Software: GovDash GovDash is the AI system for winning government contracts. It unifies five modules: Sourcing for opportunity tracking, Capture for pursuit strategy, Pricer for financial modeling, Proposal for proposal development, and Contract for post-award management. The AI agent Dash and the Data Library run across all of them, so intelligence built during capture flows into pricing, and past performance stored in the Data Library surfaces automatically when proposal sections are drafted. On the criteria that shaped these rankings, GovDash covers considerable ground. The Outline Agent, now generally available, autonomously generates compliant proposal outlines by parsing Section L and mapping requirements from solicitation documents without manual prompting. Compliance matrices update automatically when amendments drop. GovDash Pricer extracts CLINs, LCATs, and budget signals directly from solicitation sections, eliminating re-entry. Capture data auto-generates executive gate review presentations. Every AI-sourced citation traces back to a document in the Data Library. On security: Azure GovCloud hosting, NIST SP 800-171 and CMMC alignment, and confirmed FedRAMP Ready status. Full FedRAMP Authorization has not yet been achieved, so teams with ATO-dependent requirements should verify current status before committing. Teams using GovDash report up to 60% reduction in proposal development time. GovDash was built as one integrated system, not assembled through acquisitions. Every module shares the same data layer from day one, so capture intelligence compounds into sharper proposals, and every contract won makes future bids stronger. Procurement Sciences Procurement Sciences is an AI-powered RFP software built for government contractors. It focuses on proposal development workflows, helping teams respond to federal solicitations faster by using AI to analyze RFPs, identify compliance requirements, and generate draft content grounded in past performance data. What It Does Well Proposal teams can upload a solicitation and get a compliance matrix generated from Sections L and M, reducing the manual effort required to set up a response framework before writing begins. The AI drafting capability pulls from a library of past proposals, résumés, and project summaries, so generated content reflects the contractor's actual experience, not generic filler. It supports multi-user collaboration, allowing capture managers, writers, and reviewers to work inside the same document environment without version-control headaches. Where It Falls Short Procurement Sciences is a proposal-focused tool. It covers the writing and compliance phases well, but contractors who need pipeline tracking, opportunity scoring, pricing support, or contract management will need separate systems to cover those gaps. If your team is managing the full BD lifecycle, that fragmentation adds up quickly in both time and coordination overhead. See how Procurement Sciences vs GovDash compares across the full pursuit lifecycle. Rohirrim Rohirrim is an AI-powered RFP response tool built for government contractors. It focuses on helping BD and proposal teams respond faster to federal solicitations by pulling from a library of pre-approved content and past proposals. The software reads incoming RFPs, identifies relevant sections, and surfaces reusable content blocks your team has already written and approved. This cuts down the time spent hunting through shared drives or old proposal folders for the right past performance write-up or capability statement. Who It Works Best For Rohirrim fits smaller GovCon teams that need a focused response tool without a heavy implementation lift. It works well if your primary bottleneck is content retrieval and first-draft speed, not end-to-end capture or contract management. The content library builds over time as you add approved materials, so teams that already have a body of past proposals get value faster than those starting from scratch. It does not carry pipeline data, pricing, or compliance tracking alongside proposal work, so you will need separate tools if those are part of your workflow. Setup is relatively light compared to full-suite GovCon systems, which makes it accessible for teams without dedicated IT resources. The trade-off is scope. Rohirrim vs GovDash covers this trade-off in depth. If you are managing capture planning, bid/no-bid decisions, teaming, or contract performance in the same workflow, you will be stitching it together with other tools manually. Responsive Responsive is a widely used RFP software vendor with a broad feature set built around response management. It covers RFP responses, security questionnaires, and proposals, with a content library that teams can draw from to reuse approved answers across submissions. The tool is widely used in commercial sales environments where speed and content reuse matter most. Teams managing high-volume RFP workflows across industries like SaaS, financial services, and healthcare tend to get the most out of it. Where It Falls Short for Government Contractors For GovCon teams, Responsive was built for commercial procurement rhythms, not federal ones. It has no native understanding of FAR/DFARS compliance structures , Sections L and M, or the compliance matrix workflows that define federal proposal work. Content reuse works well when your submissions follow a predictable format, but federal RFPs rarely do. Section-by-section shredding tied to FAR/DFARS requirements is not something Responsive handles out of the box, which means your team is still doing that compliance matrix mapping manually . There is no pipeline or capture management built in, so the tool only covers one slice of the BD lifecycle. Pricing support for government-specific structures like CLINs, wrap rates, or BOEs is absent. If your team works exclusively in commercial markets and needs a fast, content-reuse-driven RFP tool, Responsive is a reasonable fit. For contractors managing federal solicitations, the gap between what it offers and what federal work requires is wide enough to matter. RocketDocs RocketDocs is a proposal management solution built primarily for commercial industries like insurance, banking, and financial services. It focuses on RFP response automation using a content library and AI-assisted answer suggestions to help teams respond faster to incoming RFPs. For commercial teams fielding high volumes of similar RFPs, RocketDocs can reduce response time by centralizing approved content and surfacing relevant answers. The product is reasonably well-suited to organizations with stable, repeatable content needs. Where It Falls Short for Government Contractors GovCon work has requirements that RocketDocs was not built around. A few gaps worth knowing: The content library works well for reusing boilerplate, but it has no native understanding of FAR/DFARS compliance requirements, Section L/M structure, or the compliance matrix logic that federal proposals require. There is no pipeline or capture management layer, so teams still need separate tools to track opportunities before the RFP drops. Pricing support is absent, meaning price to win in government contracting strategy and cost volume development happen entirely outside the system. Federal-specific workflows like past performance narratives tied to CPARS data or staffing plans structured around LCATs are not supported natively. If your team responds to commercial RFPs at volume and needs a straightforward content reuse system, RocketDocs is a reasonable option. For contractors managing federal solicitations with compliance requirements, Section-by-Section response structures, and interagency workflows, the fit is narrow. Feature Comparison Table of RFP Software Here is a comparison table of key features across the five RFP software picks covered in this post. Use it as a quick reference when weighing which solution fits your team's workflow, contract volume, and compliance requirements. Why GovDash Is the Best RFP Software for Government Contractors GovDash is built for government contractors, which makes it a different category of RFP software compared to the general-purpose tools on this list. Most RFP software treats government solicitations like any other document. GovDash parses Sections C, H, L, and M, builds the compliance matrix automatically, and surfaces relevant past performance from your Data Library so your team starts on strategy instead of setup. GovDash is the right fit for contractors managing complex federal work who need a purpose-built AI system, not a repurposed commercial proposal tool with a GovCon skin on top. Final Thoughts on RFP Software Options for GovCon Teams The comparison comes down to scope. Point tools handle one slice of the process well, but federal work rarely fits in one slice. The critical question is whether you need FAR/DFARS compliance logic and Section L/M parsing, because only the GovCon-specific tools on this list handle those natively. title: LinkedIn Newsletter for Founders: When It Builds Pipeline and When It Becomes Noise
summary: A LinkedIn newsletter can turn founder expertise into a durable audience, but only when it has a sharp point of view and a reason to exist beyond reposting content.
body_text: LinkedIn Newsletter for Founders: When It Builds Pipeline and When It Becomes Noise ‍ ‍ A LinkedIn newsletter sounds like an obvious move for a founder. ‍ ‍ You already have ideas. LinkedIn already has the audience. Subscribers get notified when you publish. The content lives longer than a normal post. In theory, it should be the clean bridge between founder-led LinkedIn content and a more durable owned audience. ‍ ‍ In practice, most founder newsletters become noise. ‍ ‍ They launch with a broad title, publish two generic editions, then turn into a dumping ground for company updates, podcast recaps, and long posts that should have stayed short. The founder feels like they added another content channel. The audience feels like they subscribed to another obligation. ‍ ‍ A LinkedIn newsletter only works when it has a job. For founders, that job is not to become a media company. It is to deepen trust with the exact people who need repeated exposure to the founder's judgment before they buy, invest, refer, or hire. ‍ ‍ This guide explains when founders should start a LinkedIn newsletter, what it should be about, how it should fit with normal LinkedIn posting, and how to keep it from becoming another content treadmill. ‍ ‍ What Is a LinkedIn Newsletter? ‍ ‍ A LinkedIn newsletter is a recurring article series published natively on LinkedIn. Members and Pages can publish newsletters around a specific topic, and people can subscribe to receive future editions. ‍ ‍ That sounds tactical, but the strategic question is more important: why would someone want a recurring edition from this founder? ‍ ‍ The answer cannot be, because we need another place to post content. A newsletter asks the audience for more commitment than a post. A post can earn attention once. A newsletter asks for permission to keep showing up. ‍ ‍ That permission has to be earned with a clear promise. The newsletter should help the reader understand a market, solve a recurring problem, make better decisions, or see patterns they would not see without the founder's perspective. ‍ ‍ If the founder cannot name that promise in one sentence, the newsletter is not ready. ‍ ‍ When a LinkedIn Newsletter Makes Sense for a Founder ‍ ‍ A LinkedIn newsletter makes sense when the founder has three things already working. ‍ ‍ First, the founder has a repeatable point of view. A newsletter needs a narrow enough lane that subscribers know what they are signing up for. If one edition is about hiring, the next is about fundraising, the next is about AI, and the next is a product launch, the audience cannot form a habit around it. ‍ ‍ Second, the founder has enough raw material. The best newsletters are built from sales calls, customer conversations, product decisions, investor questions, market shifts, and internal debates. If the founder is not close to the market, the newsletter will drift into generic commentary. ‍ ‍ Third, the company has a business reason for deeper education. A newsletter is useful when buyers need repeated context before they act. That is common in complex B2B categories, new markets, expensive products, long sales cycles, and founder-led companies where trust in the person affects trust in the company. ‍ ‍ If those conditions are not true, keep posting first. A newsletter should be a layer on top of a working founder-led content system, not a replacement for one. ‍ ‍ What a Founder Newsletter Should Actually Do ‍ ‍ A strong founder newsletter does not try to cover everything the company cares about. It does one or two jobs extremely well. ‍ ‍ It can create market education. This works when buyers understand the pain but not the deeper cause. The founder uses the newsletter to reframe the problem, explain patterns, and make the buyer smarter before a sales conversation. ‍ ‍ It can build category conviction. This works when the company is selling into a market shift. The founder explains why the old way is breaking, what the new way requires, and what operators should change before the cost becomes obvious. ‍ ‍ It can support fundraising visibility. This works when investors need to see how the founder thinks over time. The newsletter becomes a record of market understanding, execution lessons, and category judgment. ‍ ‍ It can create sales context. This works when the sales team can send specific editions to prospects before or after conversations. A good newsletter issue can explain a problem better than a deck, because it reads like the founder thinking in public instead of the company pitching. ‍ ‍ The best newsletters are not content for content's sake. They are a trust asset that sales, fundraising, hiring, and partnerships can all use. ‍ ‍ The Biggest Mistake: Turning the Newsletter Into a Company Update Feed ‍ ‍ Company updates are not a newsletter strategy. ‍ ‍ Most people do not subscribe because they want quarterly announcements, feature releases, webinar reminders, and recap posts. They subscribe because they expect a useful perspective that helps them do their job, understand their market, or make a better decision. ‍ ‍ That does not mean a founder can never mention the company. It means the company cannot be the center of every issue. ‍ ‍ A product launch can become a strong newsletter edition if it explains the customer problem that led to the launch, the tradeoff the team made, and what the founder learned about the market. A funding announcement can become useful if it explains the category bet behind the raise and what the founder believes will change next. A customer win can work if it teaches a broader pattern other buyers can apply. ‍ ‍ The difference is framing. The weak version says, look at us. The strong version says, here is what this reveals about the problem you care about. ‍ ‍ LinkedIn Newsletter vs. LinkedIn Posts ‍ ‍ Founders should not choose between posts and newsletters. They do different jobs. ‍ ‍ Posts are discovery. They travel through the feed, test ideas quickly, create comments, drive profile views, and help the founder learn what the market reacts to. A good post can expose an idea to people who have never heard of the founder. ‍ ‍ Newsletters are depth. They give the founder more room to explain a point of view, connect ideas, and build a habit with subscribers. A newsletter is better for people who already have enough interest to opt into a recurring relationship. ‍ ‍ The workflow should move in that order. Test ideas as posts. Watch which topics create high-quality comments, saves, DMs, and sales-call mentions. Turn the strongest themes into newsletter editions. Then break each edition back into posts. ‍ ‍ This keeps the newsletter from becoming a guessing exercise. The founder is not inventing long-form topics from scratch. They are expanding ideas that already showed market signal. ‍ ‍ That is the same principle behind LinkedIn content strategy for founders : build a system that learns from the market instead of publishing into a vacuum. ‍ ‍ The Best LinkedIn Newsletter Topics for Founders ‍ ‍ The strongest newsletter topics usually sit at the intersection of buyer pain, founder expertise, and business strategy. ‍ ‍ A founder selling to revenue leaders might publish a monthly breakdown of patterns from hundreds of sales calls. A founder building infrastructure software might explain one hard technical tradeoff operators keep underestimating. A founder selling into HR might write about the hiring risks they see across customer conversations. ‍ ‍ The topic should be specific enough to attract the right reader and repel everyone else. A newsletter called Startup Lessons is too broad. A newsletter called Notes on Enterprise AI Procurement is clearer. A newsletter called Founder Updates is weak. A newsletter called What Series A Teams Get Wrong About Demand Creation is sharper. ‍ ‍ Founders should avoid topics that only create applause from peers. The newsletter should serve the market the company needs to influence, not the audience most likely to compliment the founder. ‍ ‍ If the newsletter cannot be tied to a customer pain, investor thesis, hiring narrative, or category point of view, it is probably too soft. ‍ ‍ A Practical Founder Newsletter Workflow ‍ ‍ A founder newsletter should be simple enough to sustain. ‍ ‍ Start with a monthly cadence. Weekly sounds disciplined, but most founders do not have the time or raw material to keep weekly quality high unless they already have a mature content operation. Monthly creates enough pressure to publish without forcing filler. ‍ ‍ Build each edition from one source of truth. That source might be a customer pattern, a market shift, a strong LinkedIn post, a sales objection, a board conversation, or a product decision. One issue, one core idea. ‍ ‍ Draft around the reader's decision. What should the reader understand differently after this issue? What mistake should they avoid? What conversation should they be ready to have internally? ‍ ‍ Keep the CTA light. Most newsletter issues should not hard-sell. Point readers to a deeper article, invite replies, suggest a related post, or link to a relevant page when the connection is natural. When every issue asks for a demo, the newsletter becomes an ad. ‍ ‍ Finally, repurpose deliberately. One newsletter can become three to five LinkedIn posts, a sales follow-up asset, a blog section, and a founder voice memo prompt for future content. ‍ ‍ This is where founder content strategy matters. The newsletter should be part of the system, not another disconnected task on the founder's calendar. ‍ ‍ How to Measure a LinkedIn Newsletter ‍ ‍ A founder should not judge a newsletter only by subscriber count. ‍ ‍ Subscriber growth matters, but it is a weak metric by itself. The better question is whether the right people are subscribing and whether the newsletter is creating useful business signal. ‍ ‍ Track who subscribes when you can. Track which editions create comments, DMs, profile views, connection requests, and sales mentions. Track whether sales uses specific editions in follow-up. Track whether investors, candidates, partners, or target-account buyers reference the founder's ideas later. ‍ ‍ Also track topic performance. Which issues create the best conversations? Which ones get ignored? Which ones help explain the company's market belief? Which ones create language the team starts reusing in sales calls? ‍ ‍ The point is not to manufacture perfect attribution. The point is to understand whether the newsletter is deepening the right relationships. ‍ ‍ This connects directly to LinkedIn ROI for founders . The value of founder-led content often shows up before the conversion is visible in a dashboard. ‍ ‍ Common Mistakes With LinkedIn Newsletters ‍ ‍ The first mistake is launching too early. If the founder has not found a clear content lane, the newsletter will make the lack of focus more obvious. ‍ ‍ The second mistake is choosing a vague name. The newsletter title should tell the right reader exactly why it exists. Clever is less useful than clear. ‍ ‍ The third mistake is publishing recycled posts with no expansion. If subscribers already saw the idea in the feed, the newsletter needs to add depth, examples, or a stronger framework. ‍ ‍ The fourth mistake is using every issue as a campaign. A newsletter should create trust before it extracts attention. ‍ ‍ The fifth mistake is ignoring distribution after publishing. A newsletter edition still needs support from short posts, comments, DMs, sales follow-up, and internal enablement. Publish and pray is not a strategy. ‍ ‍ The sixth mistake is outsourcing the thinking. A team can help structure, edit, schedule, and repurpose the newsletter. The founder's real judgment still has to be inside it. ‍ ‍ How Rethoric Thinks About Founder Newsletters ‍ ‍ Rethoric's view is that a LinkedIn newsletter should never be a generic content add-on. ‍ ‍ It should come from the same source as the founder's best LinkedIn posts: real expertise, customer patterns, market conviction, and a voice that sounds like the founder instead of a marketing department. ‍ ‍ The platform mechanics matter, but they are not the hard part. The hard part is deciding what the founder is uniquely qualified to say, capturing that thinking consistently, turning it into sharp content, approving it without slowing the founder down, and measuring whether the right audience is moving closer. ‍ ‍ A newsletter can be useful inside that system. It can deepen the strongest ideas, give sales a more durable asset, and give subscribers a reason to stay close to the founder's thinking. ‍ ‍ But if the founder's normal LinkedIn content is generic, the newsletter will be generic too. Longer does not mean sharper. Recurring does not mean valuable. The system has to start with the founder's actual point of view. ‍ ‍ The Bottom Line on LinkedIn Newsletters for Founders ‍ ‍ A LinkedIn newsletter can be a strong founder-led growth asset when it gives the right audience a recurring reason to trust the founder's judgment. ‍ ‍ It should not be a company update feed, a recycled post archive, or a vanity subscriber project. It should be a focused, recurring explanation of the market, the buyer problem, or the category shift the founder understands better than most people. ‍ ‍ Start with posts. Find the themes that create real market signal. Turn the strongest ideas into newsletter editions. Use those editions across sales, fundraising, hiring, and content. Measure whether the right people move closer. ‍ ‍ If you want a founder-led LinkedIn system with strategy, capture, approvals, scheduling, engagement, tagging, mobile review, and analytics, see how Rethoric works with founders .
